title: When Graph Structure Provably Helps Classification: Non-Asymptotic Recovery Guarantees
claim: Sweeping a single regularization parameter continuously moves the solution from raw input through the true structure to a trivial collapsed solution.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, gold arrow axes marking parameter sweep
description: Two side-by-side panels, each topped by a gold arrow showing a parameter increasing. The left panel shows four square matrices for tau going from 0 to infinity. The first is the noisy adjacency matrix A, a sparse blue-and-white pattern with block structure. The next is a similar but cleaner matrix. The third is a clean block-diagonal indicator, and the last is entirely blank. A green brace underneath is labeled 'The solution of (1) for varying tau'. The right panel, with gamma going from 0 to infinity, starts with grey scatter points that are the data features. Starred centroids with small colored circles then merge into larger shaded ellipses, ending in one large blue ellipse around all points. A caption notes that the stars are the solution of (3) and the shaded regions are the recovered classes. The eye goes first to the blue matrices, then to the colored ellipses.
caption: The effect of the rank parameter $\tau$ (left) and the fusion parameter $\gamma$ (right) in problems [ref] and [ref]. As $\tau$ grows, the optimal $\bL^\star$ collapses from the adjacency $\bA$ to a block-diagonal cluster indicator and finally to zero. As $\gamma$ grows, the optimal centroids collapse from one-per-point to the true clusters and finally to a single point.
abstract: The joint use of graph structure and node-specific information is central to transductive node classification, yet a fundamental theoretical question remains: when does graph structure actually help? We provide the first deterministic, non-asymptotic, distribution-free answer to this question. We build on nuclear-norm graph clustering and generalized convex clustering. Our formulation of the latter incorporates node features, partial labels, and general convex loss functions, making it suitable for transductive node classification. We analyze each problem separately to characterize when graph structure alone, or node information alone, is sufficient for perfect recovery. We then formulate a unified convex optimization problem through a shared atomic norm representation and prove that combining the two sources expands the range of conditions under which perfect recovery is guaranteed beyond what either source alone can certify. This shows when node information can improve clustering and graph structure can improve classification.
